original_question: Let L be a finite field of characteristic p such that the extension degree [L : F_p] is a power of two. For every invertible exponent s on L, is it impossible for the reduced Fourier spectrum of the power permutation x -> x^s to have exactly three distinct values? The paper notes that this is already proved for p = 2 and p = 3, so the open case is p > 3.
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1 in Section 1 (the Helleseth three-valued conjecture), with its intended scope clarified by Proposition 1.2 and Theorem 1.3.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper's main target: the conjecture that when L is a finite field with [L : F_p] a power of 2, no invertible exponent s should give a three-valued reduced Fourier spectrum for the power permutation x -> x^s. It also correctly notes the paper's status update that the conjecture is already proved for p = 2 and p = 3, so the unresolved case is p > 3.
missing_details: The paper formulates the problem in terms of the spectrum of an invertible exponent; to be stand-alone, you should define that spectrum explicitly.
You should define an invertible exponent s over L as a positive integer with gcd(s, |L^times|) = gcd(s, |L|-1) = 1, equivalently so that x -> x^s permutes L.
You should define the canonical additive character mu_L of L, for example mu_L(x) = exp(2 pi i Tr_{L/F_p}(x)/p).
You should define the Fourier coefficients by W_{L,s}(a) = sum_{x in L} mu_L(x^s - a x) (or the equivalent Fourier-transform notation used in the paper).
You should state that the reduced Fourier spectrum means the set of out-of-phase coefficients {W_{L,s}(a) : a in L^times}, i.e. a runs over nonzero field elements.
To match the paper's terminology, 'three-valued' should mean that this reduced spectrum assumes exactly three distinct values as a ranges over L^times.

If you want the question to reflect the nearby paper context, you should mention that Proposition 1.2 introduces V_L(s), the minimum p-adic valuation of the Fourier coefficients, and proves the bound 2 V_L(s) <= [L : F_p] under the power-of-2 degree hypothesis.
To be fully paper-faithful, the relation to Theorem 1.3 should be stated precisely: that theorem proves Conjecture 1.1 for p = 2 and p = 3, which is why only p > 3 remains open.
refined_question: Let L be a finite field of characteristic p, let q = |L|, let mu_L(x) = exp(2 pi i Tr_{L/F_p}(x)/p) be the canonical additive character of L, and let s be an invertible exponent over L, meaning gcd(s, q - 1) = 1, so that x -> x^s is a permutation of L. For each a in L define W_{L,s}(a) = sum_{x in L} mu_L(x^s - a x), and let the reduced Fourier spectrum of x -> x^s be the set {W_{L,s}(a) : a in L^times}. If [L : F_p] is a power of 2, is it true that this reduced spectrum can never have exactly three distinct values? In other words, does Conjecture 1.1 hold for all remaining cases p > 3, given that the paper proves it already for p = 2 and p = 3?
justification: The draft is aiming at the paper's Conjecture 1.1, not a broader neighboring problem. Proposition 1.2 gives the valuation bound that is specifically designed for the power-of-2 extension-degree setting, and Theorem 1.3 is the paper's stated partial resolution showing the conjecture for p = 2 and p = 3. So the sharp paper-faithful reformulation is exactly the three-valued-spectrum impossibility question for invertible exponents over finite fields L with [L : F_p] a power of 2, written with the Fourier/Weil-sum notation made explicit.
